_what: Possible patterns: the same kind of thing as the patterns beside them, but ones nobody has proved yet. Each says what is probably happening, why that is likely, what the map already proves nearby, and what would turn it into cases or kill it. None of them is evidence, none names a person, and none is counted in any figure on this map.

items.title: The firms racing to plug in data centres, inside the bodies that decide grid connections
items.claim: The companies building data centres are probably reaching the small bodies that decide grid connections, tariffs and siting, because a single signature there is now worth billions.
items.rule: The mechanism is already proved in the same sector and the same country, at a time when the prize was far smaller. What has changed is the size of the decision, not the size of the body taking it: an interconnection place in the queue, or a tariff written for one customer, is still settled by a handful of appointees on a state commission or inside a grid operator.
items.conditions: A connection decision can move years of revenue and is often taken without a public hearing. The same companies that want the connection also fund the commissioners' appointing politicians, and the staff who model the grid move between the operator and the firms queuing for it.
items.documented: The map holds FirstEnergy's 60 million dollar network for an Ohio bailout law, and the 4.3 million it paid to the man who then became Ohio's utility regulator. It also holds the revolving door at the top of the same sector: a fracking chief who became United States energy secretary, and an E.ON subsidiary chief who became Germany's energy minister.
items.would_show: An inspector-general or state commission investigation into an interconnection or tariff decision, an ethics finding against a commissioner, or a leaked connection agreement with the terms in it.
items.would_refute: The large connection decisions turning out to be made on a published formula, with the queue and the exceptions open to inspection.

items.title: Scam compounds inside the immigration desks, police and zone authorities that should close them
items.claim: The operators of industrial fraud compounds are probably holding the immigration officers, police commanders and special-zone authorities of several South East Asian states, because a compound cannot run without people crossing borders and nobody raiding the gate.
items.rule: This is the shape the map already proves in three of the countries concerned, and a compound needs more official cover than a drug shipment does: staff trafficked in, victims kept in, money moved out, and a perimeter nobody enters.
items.conditions: Many compounds sit in special economic zones or border enclaves with their own authorities, their own security and their own entry rules, where the body that licenses the zone is also the body that would have to raid it.
items.documented: The map holds a Chinese citizen elected mayor of the Philippine town where an offshore gaming hub operated; the builders of a Myanmar scam city working with the army's Karen border force; an online gambling network reported to be protected by a Thai deputy police chief; and 80 Thai immigration officers charged over Chinese crime groups.
items.would_show: A prosecution naming a zone authority or an immigration post, an Interpol or United Nations operation with arrests of officials, or a defector's account that names the arrangement rather than the camp.
items.would_refute: Raids and prosecutions that reach the operators while the officials around them turn out to have been bypassed rather than bought.

items.title: Gold buyers and refiners inside central banks and mining ministries
items.claim: The networks that move artisanal gold are probably inside the central banks that buy it and the ministries that licence its export, because gold is the laundering route that needs a state signature to become clean.
items.rule: Unlike cocaine, gold has to be made legal somewhere: a refinery needs an export permit, and a central bank purchase programme turns informal metal into reserves. That signature is the thing worth buying, and the map already proves it being bought in two countries.
items.conditions: Several producing states buy gold through the central bank or a state agent at a set price, and the same small set of officials sign the export permits. The sums are large enough to matter to a national balance sheet, which makes the arrangement politically protected rather than merely corrupt.
items.documented: The map holds the United States and United Kingdom sanctioning Kamlesh Pattni over bribes in Zimbabwe's gold trade, a United States Treasury finding that Zimbabwe's president shields gold and diamond smugglers and takes payments from them, and United States charges that the Mohamed gold family bribed Guyanese officials.
items.would_show: A Treasury or sanctions designation naming a refinery together with a central bank officer, a parliamentary audit of a gold purchase programme, or a prosecution over export permits.
items.would_refute: Audits of the purchase programmes finding the metal and the permits accounted for.

items.title: Ship registries, where a sovereign signature is handed to a private office abroad
items.claim: The fleets that carry sanctioned oil are probably inside the registries that flag them, because a registration and a class certificate are what let a tanker trade, and many registries are run as a business from another country entirely.
items.rule: This is the one possible pattern here with no case on the map at all, which is why it is worth stating. The structure is unusually exposed: a state's power to register ships is frequently delegated to a private operator overseas, paid per vessel, with the flag state itself having little capacity to supervise what is registered in its name.
items.conditions: A registration is a single decision that confers a nationality. The customer wants speed and discretion, the operator is paid by volume, and the state whose flag it is may learn what it has flagged only when a vessel is detained.
items.documented: Nothing directly. What the map does prove is the adjacent thing: that where a state function is run for profit by outsiders it gets used for them, from creditors' agents running a country's customs to the sale of passports and diplomatic posts.
items.would_show: A flag state's own audit or a criminal case against registry staff, an International Maritime Organization finding on a registry operating without authority, or a detention report that traces a false registration back to the office that issued it.
items.would_refute: Registries publishing what they refuse and why, with beneficial ownership checked before a flag is granted.

items.title: Carbon and offset brokers inside the forestry ministries that sign over the trees
items.claim: The brokers assembling forest carbon projects are probably reaching the same forestry ministries and officials that timber money has always reached, because a project needs one ministerial signature over an area larger than any logging concession.
items.rule: The map proves that timber buyers reach the officials who control forests. A carbon project asks for the same thing from the same office - rights over standing trees for decades - and is harder to check, because what is being sold is an absence of logging rather than a shipment anyone can count.
items.conditions: Project rights are often granted over customary land by a ministry that also certifies the baseline the credits are measured against, in states where the forestry office has long been the one worth paying.
items.documented: The map holds Malaysian loggers reported to fund Solomon Islands MPs, a logging boss convicted of trying to bribe Solomon Islands customs, and logging firms paying South Sudan's army, security and intelligence officers.
items.would_show: A national audit or a registry's own investigation cancelling a project with a finding about the officials who approved it, or a prosecution over the baseline.
items.would_refute: Project approvals and baselines being published with the land rights verified independently, and cancellations turning on bad science rather than bought signatures.

items.title: Security companies taking the adviser's chair, the way one of them already has
items.claim: Other armed security companies are probably taking the post beside a president or inside a defence ministry in exchange for concessions, because one of them has already shown that the arrangement works and survives.
items.rule: The map proves the full mechanism once, in detail: a company's man appointed as a president's security adviser, and the same company's firms granted mining permits in the same country. A model that has been demonstrated, paid for and not reversed is the kind that gets copied, and the states that bought it are not the only ones short of soldiers.
items.conditions: A government fighting an insurgency can pay in minerals rather than money, and the contract that provides the soldiers can also provide the official who writes the next contract.
items.documented: The map holds Wagner's Valery Zakharov appointed security adviser to the Central African Republic's president, Wagner firms granted mining permits there with a report that they shaped the mining code, and Prigozhin's strategists paying Madagascar presidential candidates.
items.would_show: A contract, an appointment decree or a United Nations panel finding that names a company's employee in a government post, and a concession granted to the same company.
items.would_refute: The successor companies turning out to be paid in cash on published contracts, with no personnel placed in government.

items.title: Medicine makers inside the agencies that approve drugs, not only the hospitals that buy them
items.claim: The companies that have been caught paying the doctors and ministries which buy their products are probably also reaching the smaller bodies that approve and register them, where one decision opens a whole national market.
items.rule: Every proven case on the map is at the buying end - tenders, auctions, prescribing doctors. Approval is the larger prize and the softer target: fewer people, less publicity, and a decision that cannot be competed away afterwards.
items.conditions: A national medicines agency may be a few dozen assessors, often part-time and often also in clinical practice or on a ministry commission, deciding whether a product can be sold at all.
items.documented: The map holds Alexion paying doctors who sat on Turkey's health ministry commissions and chief non-staff specialist advisers to Russia's health ministry; Teva paying a Russian official to win state health auctions; Fresenius paying state doctors in Saudi Arabia, Morocco and Turkiye; and Indian medical colleges alleged to have paid health ministry staff.
items.would_show: A regulator's own integrity case, a Securities and Exchange Commission order that names an approval or registration rather than a sale, or an assessor prosecuted.
items.would_refute: Approval files and assessors' interests being published, with reviews repeatable by someone outside the agency.

items.title: Exchanges and payment firms inside the regulators that licence them
items.claim: The exchanges and payment companies that need a licence are probably reaching the regulators that grant it, in the small jurisdictions that compete to be where they register.
items.rule: The map already proves the two halves separately: a regulator's own man arriving from the industry he then regulated, and a bank regulator paid to look away. A licence that lets a firm serve customers worldwide from a jurisdiction of a few hundred thousand people is a bigger prize than either, taken by a smaller body.
items.conditions: Licensing competition is explicit - states advertise their regimes to attract these firms - and the regulator that grants a licence is also the one that would have to withdraw it, in places where that office and the industry share a very small professional world.
items.documented: The map holds a crypto adviser who became chair of the United States Securities and Exchange Commission, after which crypto lawsuits were dropped, and Stanford paying Antigua's bank regulator to look away.
items.would_show: A licensing scandal with an official named, a regulator's staff prosecuted, or an audit of why one firm's licence survived a failure that closed others.
items.would_refute: Licence decisions and their conditions being published, with refusals and withdrawals explained.

items.title: Distant-water fishing fleets inside the ministries and coast guards that licence and police them
items.claim: The fleets that fish other countries' waters are probably inside the fisheries ministries that sell the quotas and the coast guards and observers who are supposed to check them.
items.rule: The map proves the quota end of this once, in full: a foreign fleet's money reaching the circle around a fisheries minister in exchange for quotas. The enforcement end is the same arrangement one step down - an observer who signs the log, a patrol that is elsewhere - and it is cheaper to buy.
items.conditions: A small coastal state may licence a fleet worth more than its own budget, with the catch verified by one observer at sea and the water patrolled by a handful of vessels.
items.documented: The map holds Fishrot, where the Icelandic company Samherji paid the circle around Namibian ministers for fishing quotas, and Mozambique's finance minister paid in the tuna bonds deal.
items.would_show: A prosecution or commission naming an observer programme, a licensing office or a patrol commander, or a flag state's audit of its own fleet's licences.
items.would_refute: Licence registers, catch data and observer deployments being published and reconciling with each other.
